web_title: 9. Both Sides of the Aisle, Likely Outcomes & No-FOMO Action Plan
question: Given what the business has shown, what the price assumes and what the tape says, is there a reason to own Stallion now, and if not, at what price?

web_blocks.html: This chapter turns the evidence into a decision. We set out the strongest case for owning Stallion and the strongest case against it, put probabilities on the three outcomes from chapter 7, and state the action for the next two years. The answer is WAIT_FOR_SUPPORT. The business is conditional, the price already assumes a plant ramp that has not happened, and the stock is in Stage 4. We do not reject the company outright. The plants could work, and the bull case is large. We also do not buy at ₹187.

The strongest bull argument is that management has delivered on its last set of numbers. FY26 revenue was ₹430.7 crore and profit after tax ₹43.8 crore, and operating cash flow of ₹39.4 crore met the ₹40 crore level the company had pointed to [1][3]. The balance sheet is far stronger than it was before the rights issue: net cash is about ₹400 crore against ₹34 crore of borrowings [1]. A company with that cash and a plan to add capacity does not face a funding crisis on the next plant.

The plants are real capacity, even though they are late. The 10,000-tonne R-32 plant at Bhilwara has moved from July 2026 to the end of December 2026 [8][9]. The Khalapur helium unit is expected to run at about 20 percent utilisation next year, and the Mambattu blend plant is due to start at the end of 2026 [9]. Late is not the same as absent. The regulatory frame supports the core product: under the Kigali Amendment, India's HFC consumption is due to be frozen from 1 January 2028, which limits supply growth in the market as a whole and favours producers who already have capacity [17]. If the plants start on time and the margin returns, the FY28 bull case is arithmetically possible.

The strongest bear argument is that the business has not yet shown it can earn steady profits on the capacity it already has. Operating margin was 18.2 percent in the June 2026 quarter and 2.2 percent in the September quarter, with a tax charge of 57 percent in the latter [14]. Management called June a special quarter [8]. The September quarter has no explanation in the sources we reached. Operating cash flow was negative in FY24 and FY25, and the cash conversion cycle is about 180 days [1][6].

The structural risks are concentrated. Refrigerant gases were 81.9 percent of product sales in FY24 [25]. Import costs were 85 percent of revenue in the six months to September 2024, and China supplied 92.97 percent of those imports [6]. The company has no long-term supply contracts with those suppliers [6]. Ten customers accounted for 77.3 percent of revenue in the same period [6]. A single supply problem or a single lost customer reaches most of the business at once.

Then the price and the tape. The reverse DCF in chapter 7 says the market is paying for about 20 percent profit growth for ten years [14]. The stock is in Stage 4 and below most of its averages [32]. And promoter holding fell by about 20 points in six months, to 47.8 percent, without an explanation in the filings we reviewed [15]. None of these facts makes the business a failure. Together they make the outcome wide, and a wide outcome needs a price that pays you for the width.

web_blocks.takeaway: Both cases are real. The bull case is strongest on capacity and cash, and the bear case is strongest on margins, concentration and the tape. Neither side wins on the balance of the evidence today, which is why the answer is to wait for a price that pays for the uncertainty.

web_blocks.html: We weight the three FY28 scenarios from chapter 7 by probability. The bear case gets 35 percent, because the plants have already slipped once and the latest margin is weak. The base case gets 45 percent, because it assumes the R-32 plant starts and sales grow about 27 percent a year, below management's guidance. The bull case gets 20 percent, because it needs sales of about ₹1,100 crore in FY28 and a 14 percent margin, both of which the company has not yet delivered [9].

web_blocks.caption: Probability-weighted FY28 values per share at a 30 times multiple plus net cash of ₹34.43 a share, against the price of ₹187.12 [1][9][14]
web_blocks.takeaway: The weighted value is 21 percent above today's price. Spread over two years, that is about 10 percent a year, below our 12.5 percent cost of equity. At ₹187 the stock does not pay us enough for the risk we are taking.

web_blocks.the_number: A probability-weighted two-year value of ₹226.9 a share, about 21 percent above ₹187.12, or roughly 10.1 percent a year.
web_blocks.how_calculated: Each scenario value is FY28 net profit per share multiplied by 30, plus net cash of ₹34.43 a share. The three values are weighted 35, 45 and 20 percent. The annual return is the square root of the ratio of the weighted value to the price, less one.
web_blocks.the_inputs: Net cash of ₹34.43 a share from the March 2026 balance sheet [1]; an implied 11.61 crore shares [14]; FY28 revenue and net margin for each scenario from chapter 7 [9].
web_blocks.the_range: Bear value ₹68 at 15 times earnings, against ₹101 at 30 times. At a 15 times bear multiple the weighted value is about ₹215, roughly 15 percent above the price.
web_blocks.if_off: If the bear probability rose to 50 percent and the bull fell to 15 percent, the weighted value would be about ₹197, only about 5 percent above the price, or 2.6 percent a year. The stock would still sit below the 12.5 percent hurdle. The call would not change, but the margin of error would shrink to nothing.

web_blocks.html: The hurdle sets the price. Compounded at 12.5 percent a year for two years, the required return is a multiple of about 1.27. Divide the weighted value of ₹226.9 by 1.27 and the price that delivers the hurdle is about ₹179. At ₹187, the expected return is under the hurdle. At ₹159.79, the top of the support zone, the same weighted value is 42 percent higher, about 19 percent a year, which clears the hurdle with room to spare. That gap is why the entry sits in the zone and not at today's price.

The zone call is also sensitive to the weights. From ₹159.79, a 50/35/15 weighting (bear, base, bull; assumptions) gives about 11 percent a year, below the 12.5 percent hurdle. With the bear weight held at 35 percent, the zone clears the hurdle only while the bull case keeps a weight of about 8 percent or more. The support-zone entry is therefore a bet on the plant ramp, not a discount on today's value.

web_blocks.caption: The verdict on each holding horizon for Stallion, as of 13 November 2026 [9][14][32]
rows: Stage 4, below the 10-day, 20-day, 30-week and 10-week averages; no 4-hour repair; no entry inside the no-FOMO gate.
Needs the R-32 plant started by the end of December 2026, and operating margins back in the mid-teens on a half-year basis, before the cash case improves.
The business has a credible product and a long regulatory runway, but ten years of 20 percent profit growth has not started. The reverse DCF makes that the central question.
web_blocks.takeaway: The three horizons agree. The business may compound over the long term, the medium-term test is the plant ramp, and the short-term setup does not support new money at today's price.

web_blocks.html: Why not reject it? The FY26 targets were met, the balance sheet is strong and the plants have real capacity behind them. That is not a fundamental failure, and we do not treat it as one. Why not buy it now? The price is 17 percent above the support zone, the stock is in Stage 4, and the expected return at this price is below the hurdle. The honest answer is wait, with a price and a set of events that would change it.

The call moves to an entry only when a daily close inside ₹155.07 to ₹159.79 holds on a closing basis, with the ₹152.30 stop intact and the R-32 plant still on track for the end of December 2026. A weekly close under ₹152.30 ends the setup.

Stallion is not held in any account in the positions ledger, so there is no sale to make and no shares to trim. The holding action is NOT_HELD. The next marginal rupee stays in cash. We do not fund a shortlist or outside name in this dossier, because the names that clear today's technical gate in the shortlist were not underwritten here and we will not force a destination for capital that is not needed.

The alert levels in the table below are for a position that does not exist yet. They are not orders. The first is a daily close inside the ₹155 to ₹160 zone with the stop intact and volume below its average. The second is a weekly close under ₹152.30, which would end the setup. The third is a daily close above the 50-day average at ₹209.16, which would start a re-test of the trend. Each alert is a reason to re-run the Stage 2 scan and the evidence checks in this dossier, not a reason to buy on its own.

web_blocks.intro: If the zone holds and the setup is confirmed, the position is sized from the stop distance, not from conviction. The conviction tier is TIER_3, and the stop is 152.30 against an entry of about 159.79.

web_blocks.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
paragraphs: The most useful thing this dossier does is make the price of waiting visible. At ₹187 the expected return over two years is about 10 percent a year. At ₹159 it is about 19. The business has not changed between those two numbers. Only the price has, and the price is the thing you control.

If the plants start on time, the margin comes back, and the stock repairs its averages, the call moves up and the price may not wait for you. We accept that risk. A stock that has already gone up on a good story is a poor buy when the story is still unproven, and a better buy after the proof arrives at a price that still pays for it.

book_paragraphs: This is the chapter where the arguments meet, and I want to give each side its best case before I give my answer. The bull case is that the company has kept its promises so far. FY26 revenue was about 431 crore, profit was about 44 crore, and operating cash flow of about 39 crore met the level the company had set. The balance sheet has about 400 crore of net cash after the rights issue. A company with that cash and a plan to add capacity is not in a funding crisis.

The plants are late, but they are not gone. The R-32 plant has moved to the end of December 2026. The helium unit will run at low utilisation next year. The bull case says these are the first steps of a ramp, and that the regulatory freeze on hydrofluorocarbons from 2028 will favour the producer who already has capacity. If that ramp arrives on time, the 2028 bull case is arithmetically possible.

The bear case is equally direct. The business has not yet shown that it can earn steady profit on the capacity it already has. The June quarter had an operating margin of about 18 percent, and the September quarter had about 2 percent, with a tax charge of 57 percent. Operating cash flow was negative in two of the last three years. Refrigerant gases are most of the sales, imports are most of the costs, and the company has no long-term supply contracts with its main supplier country. Ten customers are about three-quarters of revenue.

The price already assumes the good version of the story. The reverse DCF says the market is paying for about 20 percent profit growth for a decade. The stock is in Stage 4, and it has fallen below most of its averages. The promoter stake fell by about twenty points in six months, and the filings I read do not say why. Those facts do not make this a failed business. They make the outcome wide, and a wide outcome should be paid for with a lower entry.

I put probabilities on the three outcomes. Thirty-five percent for the bear case, 45 for the base and 20 for the bull. Weighted, the two-year value is about 227 rupees, which is 21 percent above today's price. That sounds like a yes until you annualise it. It works out to about 10 percent a year, below the 12.5 percent return I require for this kind of risk. At 187 rupees, the stock does not pay enough.

The number that changes the answer is the price. At about 179 rupees the weighted value would just meet the hurdle. At the top of the support zone, about 160 rupees, the same weighted value is about 42 percent higher, or roughly 19 percent a year. That is why the entry is in the zone and not at today's price.

Let me say how I would size the idea, because sizing is where investors get hurt even when the analysis is right. The position is not sized on conviction. It is sized on the distance between the entry and the stop. From the top of the zone the stop sits about 4.7 percent below the entry, so a given amount of risk supports a much larger position than it would if the stop were 15 percent away. That keeps the loss small when the setup fails, which it sometimes does, and it puts the most capital where the stop is closest.

The probability weights are the most judgement-heavy part of the work, and I want to be open about them. I gave the bear case 35 percent because the plants have already slipped once and the margin in the latest quarter is weak. I gave the bull case 20 percent because it needs about 1,100 crore of sales in FY28, more than two and a half times FY26. If you think the bull case is more likely, the weighted value rises and the zone becomes more attractive. If you think the bear case is more likely, the reverse holds and the stop matters more.

What would change my mind about the bear case is simple to name. A clean R-32 start by the end of December, a second quarter with a margin back in the teens, and a management explanation of the September quarter that holds up when the numbers arrive would each move probability from the bear case toward the base. What would change my mind about the bull case is also simple. A slip of the R-32 start into next year, or a second weak quarter, would move probability away from it.

Cash is not free to hold. If the rupee sitting in cash could buy a stock that clears every gate today, waiting has a cost. The shortlist has names that clear the technical gate today, and this dossier has not underwritten them, so I cannot say they are better. The discipline is the same for each. Fund a name from cash only when it has passed the evidence review and the price gate. Stallion gets no special exemption from that rule, and neither does any other name.

The alerts are not orders, and the reason matters. An alert tells you that the conditions for a fresh check have been met. It does not tell you that the stock will rise. The first alert, a daily close in the zone with volume at or below its average, starts the work of checking the evidence again. The second, a weekly close under 152.30, ends the setup. The third, a close above the 50-day average, starts a re-test of the trend. Treat each as a prompt to think, and make the decision with the evidence in front of you.

Suppose the price reaches 159 next month and the R-32 plant has not started. The discipline still says to look before buying. The zone and the plant are two separate conditions, and the zone alone is not enough. The stock may simply be falling further. In that case the right answer is to watch for a base and a repair on the weekly chart, and to accept that the entry may come on a second visit to the zone. We would rather miss a move than buy into a second leg down.

So the decision is wait. Not reject, because the business is not failing and the plants could work. Not buy now, because the price is too high for the uncertainty, the tape is in decline and the expected return is below what I need. Hold the list of events in mind: the R-32 start by the end of December, a half-year margin that comes back, a weekly close back above the averages, and a price that pays for the risk. When those line up, the answer may change.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Write down the price you would pay and the event you need to see before you pay it. For Stallion the price is inside 155 to 160 rupees and the event is the plants starting. If the price arrives first and the plant does not, the answer is still wait.
